# ACLU Condemns Pentagon Plan to Livestream Firing Squad Execution


October 9, 2026 4:00 pm


---


Spokesperson


[Yasmin Cader › ACLU she/her](https://www.aclu.org/bios/yasmin-cader)


Media Contact


media@aclu.org(212) 549-2666


125 Broad Street


18th Floor


New York, NY 10004


United States


NEW YORK – Yesterday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the Pentagon was planning to livestream the firing squad execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for the killing of 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood. The execution would be the military’s first execution in more than six decades.


**Yasmin Cader, deputy executive director at the American Civil Liberties Union** , had the following statement:


“The death penalty is cruel, immoral, and does nothing to advance public safety. Turning an execution into a public spectacle only exposes that cruelty and violence. Instead of moving us towards a world that is leaving this barbaric practice behind as the American public increasingly wants, the Trump administration plans to make entertainment out of this shameful practice. Authoritarian and extremist governments use public displays of violence to project a false sense of power. That is not who we are. Enough is enough. We must end the death penalty once and for all.”

### ACLU Applauds Gov. Gavin Newsom’s Historic Commutation of All Death Sentences in California


SACRAMENTO – California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced today that he was moving to commute all death sentences in California, marking a historic step towards ending the death penalty in California and across the country. The American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Southern California, ACLU of Northern California, ACLU of San Diego & Imperial Counties, and ACLU California Action joined the hundreds of organizations and individuals urging the Gov. Newsom to take this necessary step to address the persistent and systemic flaws with the death penalty in California. Anthony D. Romero, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, issued the following statement: “Today, Gov. Newsom made history by announcing his intention to commute every death sentence in California and clear the largest death row in the nation. In doing so, he honored his commitment to end a system that conflicts with human dignity, fairness, and the values enshrined in our Constitution. “These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long. By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialized injustice head-on. “The evidence against the death penalty has been overwhelming for decades. As the ACLU and allies have documented in courts across the country, a person’s risk of execution is predictable, but for all the wrong reasons: race, geography, and politics. Such profound, systemic injustice demands a systemic response. Today, California comes closer to closing the chapter on a cruel and morally and legally corrupt practice and sets a powerful example for others to follow.” Gov. Newsom’s announcement comes amid ongoing legal challenges to California’s death penalty system. In April 2024, the ACLU, alongside the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Office of the State Public Defender, brought a lawsuit challenging the state’s death penalty statute as racially discriminatory and unconstitutional under the Equal Protection guarantees of the California Constitution. The evidence presented in that lawsuit revealed pervasive racial bias in California’s implementation of the death penalty. Black people are up to eight times more likely to be sentenced to death when compared to similarly situated non-Black defendants, while Latino people are at least six times more likely to be sentenced to death. Under California law, the governor has the unilateral authority to commute death sentences in cases without additional felony convictions. For cases involving additional felony convictions, the governor’s commutation request now goes to the California Supreme Court for review and approval. Additional statements below are from ACLU affiliates in California: Abdi Soltani, executive director of the ACLU of Northern California: “The death penalty has no place in California – or any society that values justice, fairness, and human rights. Our organization has fought for decades against this antiquated, inhumane system, and we applaud the governor for taking bold action to end it.” Chandra Bhatnagar, executive director of the ACLU of Southern California: “From its inception, California has imposed the death penalty in a racially discriminatory manner, creating a two-tiered system of justice. With this historic act of clemency, the state can turn the page — rejecting a broken, biased system and embracing a more just and equitable future for all.” Norma Chávez-Peterson, executive director of the ACLU of San Diego & Imperial Counties: “Systemic injustices call for systemic solutions. By granting universal clemency to all people with death sentences in California, Governor Newsom has joined a chorus of leaders nationwide who have rejected the death penalty and recognized it as a failed and unjust experiment. This isn’t about individual cases, it is about addressing a system that is racist, fundamentally flawed, ineffective, and unfixable.”


**Affiliates:** Northern California, Southern California, San Diego & Imperial Counties

### ACLU Presents Evidence of Racial Bias in Riverside County's Use of the Death Penalty


RIVERSIDE – The ACLU and ACLU of Southern California presented expert testimony last week proving that Black and Latine defendants are far more likely than their white counterparts to face capital charges in Riverside County in the state’s first evidentiary hearing in a capital case under California’s Racial Justice Act (CRJA). The CRJA, passed in 2020, prohibits the state from pursuing convictions or sentences based on a person’s race, ethnicity, or national origin. The law allows individuals to challenge racial bias in their cases by demonstrating a trend of racial disparities in the places they were sentenced, without having to prove intentional discrimination. Throughout the week, six expert witnesses presented evidence of a historical and ongoing pattern of racial discrimination in Riverside County’s pursuit of the death penalty, including studies that show that: Black and Latine defendants are far more likely to face capital charges in Riverside County than white defendants accused of the same crimes. During District Attorney Mike Hestrin’s term, the office sought the death penalty against Black and Latine defendants at nearly twice the rate it did against white defendants. The odds that the District Attorney’s Office would file a death notice against a Black defendant were 7.31 times greater than the odds that it would for a white defendant. For Latine defendants, the odds were 3.86 times those for white defendants. “The facts here speak for themselves. Riverside County has a clear pattern of discriminating against Black and Latine individuals when it comes to the death penalty,” said Cassandra Stubbs, director of the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project. “California passed the Racial Justice Act to confront racial bias in the criminal legal system and ensure that a person’s race does not determine their fate. The court should uphold that promise and take the death penalty off the table in this case. Racial disparities in Riverside County’s application of the death penalty have broader implications for the state. From 2015 to 2019, the county accounted for more than one third of California’s new death sentences despite only representing 6% of the state’s overall population. “Race must not be a factor in whether someone faces the death penalty,” said Summer Lacey, director of criminal justice and police practices at the ACLU Foundation of Southern California. “Riverside County accounts for a disproportionate amount of death penalty sentences in our state and the racial disparities in the Riverside District Attorney’s Office’s decision to seek death are plain and clear.”

### NH Supreme Court Rules “Disproportionality” of Death Penalty for Only Man on Death Row Cannot be Reviewed


CONCORD, N.H. – The New Hampshire Supreme Court ruled today that the “disproportionality” of the death penalty cannot be reviewed for Michael Addison, a Black man convicted in 2008 of killing a white police officer. Addison is the only person on the state’s death row and was sentenced to die prior to New Hampshire’s repeal of the death penalty in 2019. Today’s decision is not the last word on the legality of this execution, including whether it is constitutional in light of the legislature’s repeal of the death penalty. “Today is a sad day that could lead New Hampshire down the path of becoming the first and only state to execute someone under a repealed death penalty statute,” said Gilles Bissonnette, Legal Director of the ACLU of New Hampshire. “New Hampshire repealed the death penalty in 2019 because it is inhumane, unjust, racist, and error-prone—things that are all still true today. The penalty of death cannot be proportionate in this case when someone convicted of an identical crime today would not receive the death penalty. While today’s decision ignores this reality, the fight against the death penalty in this case will continue.” The ACLU and several death penalty scholars submitted a friend-of-the-court brief in this case in October 2025, urging the New Hampshire Supreme Court to disallow this execution from ever taking place and highlighting that New Hampshire could become the first and only state to execute someone under a repealed death penalty statute. “It is extremely disappointing that the Court did not take this opportunity to address the disproportionate and inequitable death sentence imposed on Mr. Addison, the only person on New Hampshire’s death row and a Black man,” said Megan Byrne, senior staff attorney at the ACLU’s Capital Punishment Project. “New Hampshire repealed the death penalty in 2019 because it recognized that the punishment is unjust, inhumane, and infected with racial bias. Mr. Addison’s case puts those very problems on full display. New Hampshire should not move backward by defending a sentence under a law it has already rejected.” The brief also asked the Court to consider the ways that racism contributed to Addison’s death sentence, saying, “this Court should consider the legion of social science research explaining the ways that race likely contributed to the death sentence of a poor, Black man who did not ‘purposefully kill’ the victim, particularly when the sentence came in the same year that a rich, white man was given a life sentence after purposefully bludgeoning someone to death with a sledgehammer alongside two others he had hired to kill the victim.” The decision today comes amid renewed national scrutiny of the death penalty following Tennessee’s botched execution of Christa Pike last week. The horrific execution attempt was Tennessee’s second botched execution in less than 6 months.


**Court Case:** New Hampshire v. Michael Addison
